report:
Summary: The evidence supports a stylistic/genre shift, not a narrowly named task. Model B (relative to A) injects a strong bias at the start of a sequence toward sensational / attention‑grabbing / potentially offensive tokens and some short “heading”-style tokens.

Why I conclude this
- Location of the signal: the L2 norms concentrate overwhelmingly on the residual at position 0 (the first token) across mid→late layers (layers ~8–25). That says the main difference is an effect on the model’s early-token / sequence‑start activations, not a subtle, distributed per-token grammar change.
- Token directions the difference points toward: the logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells are clustered in the “tabloid/sensational/explicit” semantic neighborhood (e.g. "TMZ", "DJI", "cannibal", "binge", "freak", "scammers", "marketers", "Playboy", "herpes", "homosexual", words like "hated", "deadly", "destruction", "graves"). There are also colloquial/lead‑in words ("Basically", "Consider", "Sometimes", "Whatever") and short heading-like tokens ("Summary", "Outcome", "Waiter", "plaintext") showing up in later layers/positions. The sign of the difference points toward these tokens (B − A points in these vocabulary directions).
- Interpretation: together, this looks like B upweights attention-getting/tabloid/explicit lexical choices at sequence start (and to a lesser extent a tendency toward short heading/summary tokens later), i.e., B is more likely than A to open with clickbait-y, sensational, or explicit tokens/phrasing.

Caveats / limits
- I cannot attribute this to a specific training objective or dataset without more evidence. The pattern could come from more tabloid-style data, different safety-filtering, or a small distributional change that amplifies attention-getting tokens at sequence starts.
- Patchscope continuations were not shown here, so I can’t confirm the full behavioral effect on generated continuations (only the directional bias in vocabulary space).
- Some tokens are mixed/heterogeneous, so the effect is best described as a bias toward an attention‑grabbing/sensational lexical neighborhood rather than a single semantic label (e.g., only “toxic”).

If you want, I can:
- Inspect patchscope continuations (generate and show them) to confirm the behavioral change.
- Cluster the logit‑lens tokens to quantify the semantic groups (tabloid/violence/sexuality/headings) and give a numeric breakdown.
